  "title": "Latent-Distribution Candidate Selection for Frozen World Action Models: OOD Consistency Scoring and Action-Latent Value Learning",
  "core_problem": "Pretrained WAMs generate a single action trajectory at inference and provide no mechanism to compare candidate futures. Adding planning capability currently requires one of three costly interventions: (1) full fine-tuning of the video model on robot demos (Cosmos Policy, ICLR 2026: 384–3,072 H100-hours); (2) training a separate action-conditioned world model alongside the frozen policy (GPC, RAL 2025); or (3) architectural co-design or RL loops (H-WM, GigaBrain RAMP, WAV). Fast-WAM (arXiv 2603.16666) demonstrates that action-only inference achieves 97.6% on LIBERO and 91.8% on RoboTwin at 190ms, motivating candidate generation from frozen WAM action-only inference rather than expensive video rollouts.

The VLA test-time compute literature (2025–2026) has addressed candidate selection for VLA architectures: RoVer (arXiv 2510.10975, ICLR 2026) trains a 0.2B Process Reward Model; MG-Select (arXiv 2510.05681, ICLR 2026) uses KL-divergence from a masked unconditional VLA distribution as a training-free confidence signal, achieving 168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place; Cosmos Policy (ICLR 2026) implements Best-of-N in its planning mode by generating B candidates and scoring each via a fine-tuned value function — but crucially, Cosmos Policy's authors report that a model trained only on demonstrations 'cannot correctly predict failure states' and that rollout fine-tuning is required to enable effective planning. None of these approaches exploit WAMs' unique property: joint video-action pretraining that regularizes action latents z_a to be consistent with physically plausible visual futures, forming a success-biased latent distribution.

The critical unanswered question — which VLA approaches cannot answer — is: (1) Do WAM action latents z_a, regularized by joint video-action pretraining, form a latent success distribution that is more structured and separable from failure regimes than VLA action tokens, enabling lightweight OOD-based candidate scoring without any rollout data? (2) Is this latent OOD signal more informative than action-space distributional uncertainty (MG-Select's KL signal) for candidate selection? These questions are grounded in the FAIL-Detect (arXiv 2503.08558, RSS 2025) finding that OOD detection on success-only demonstrations reliably identifies failures — but have not been applied to WAM action latents or to pre-execution candidate selection. The companion question of whether video denoising error (as opposed to latent OOD scoring) is a reliable zero-training signal is answered negatively by Cosmos Policy's own finding and by EVA (arXiv 2603.17808), which demonstrates an 'executability gap' showing that visual coherence does not predict task success.

No existing work demonstrates Best-of-N candidate selection using WAM action latents' distributional structure — either zero-training (OOD scoring) or lightweight-trained (value MLP) — without modifying any WAM weights or requiring rollout data for the zero-training path.",
  "opportunity": "UWM's independent per-modality diffusion timestep architecture (RSS 2025) natively supports action-only inference (video timestep = T, action timestep = 0), producing action latents z_a jointly pretrained with video. This creates two complementary WAM-specific approaches to candidate selection, exploiting the distributional structure of the WAM's joint video-action pretraining:

**Method 1 — Latent OOD Consistency Scoring (LOC, zero weight updates)**: Encode LIBERO-90 success demonstrations through frozen UWM in action-only mode to obtain a reference distribution {z_a^success}. Fit a lightweight density estimator — KNN-based nonconformity score (k=10) or Gaussian Mixture Model (k≤5 components) — on {z_a^success}. At inference, sample B=4–8 action-only candidates from frozen UWM, obtain latents {z_{a,1}, ..., z_{a,B}}, and score each: S_LOC(z_{a,i}) = −log p̂(z_{a,i}) (nonconformity score). Select a_{i*} = argmin_i S_LOC(z_{a,i}) (most in-distribution candidate). Total inference overhead: B × ~5ms = 20–40ms for B=4–8, significantly cheaper than video decoder passes. Cost: ~30–60 minutes to fit density estimator on encoded latents; no WAM weight updates.

Theoretical basis: (1) FAIL-Detect (RSS 2025) proves that OOD detection on success-only demonstration data reliably detects policy failures — the success-demo distribution implicitly excludes failure modes; (2) z_a regularized by joint video-action pretraining encodes physical plausibility co-varying with video futures, potentially creating a tighter success latent distribution with less success/failure overlap than VLA action tokens. LOC is WAM-specific in that this tighter latent structure is a direct consequence of joint video-action pretraining absent in VLAs. Differentiation from MG-Select: LOC scores membership in the success demonstration distribution (latent OOD density); MG-Select measures KL divergence of task-conditioned output from masked unconditional distribution (action-space distributional uncertainty). These are mechanistically distinct signals — one measures distributional membership relative to labeled success data, the other measures task-conditioning confidence.

Note on Cosmos Policy planning mode: Cosmos Policy also implements Best-of-N candidate selection — it generates B actions, predicts future states and values for each, and executes the highest-value action. However, Cosmos Policy's planning mode (a) requires fine-tuning a value function on rollout data (1,536 H100-hours for RoboCasa) because demonstration-only training 'cannot correctly predict failure states' (Cosmos Policy, 2026), and (b) queries the world model 3× and value function 5× per action (15 total forward passes per candidate) requiring parallel GPU infrastructure. LOC requires zero rollout data, zero weight updates, and ~5ms per candidate.

Note on PCS: The original approach of using video denoising error S_PCS = ||ε − ε_θ(x_{t*}, z_{a,i}, t*)||² as a zero-training quality signal is retained as a diagnostic comparison in the LOC diagnostic step (Step 1), not as a primary method. Cosmos Policy's explicit finding that demonstration-trained video priors do not reliably predict failure states, corroborated by the EVA 'executability gap' finding that visual coherence does not imply executable actions, provides strong prior evidence that raw denoising error will be a weak candidate selection signal. We include it as a secondary signal in Step 1 to report a clean negative result comparison against LOC.

**Method 2 — Action-Latent Value MLP (≤40 H100-hours training)**: A 3-layer MLP trained on WAM action latents z_a from LIBERO-90 success demonstrations AND explicitly collected failure trajectories scores each candidate via V(z_{a,i}) ∈ [0,1]. Hard argmax Best-of-N (a_{i*} = argmax_i V(z_{a,i})) is the primary result. Key hypothesis: z_a regularized by joint video-action pretraining is more linearly separable between success and failure regimes than raw action outputs or VLA action tokens (the latent geometry argument). Failure demonstrations collected via frozen UWM rollouts in simulation (~15–20 H100-hours) plus Gaussian-perturbed synthetic failures (<1 H100-hour).

**Comparison of LOC vs. Value MLP is itself a central contribution**: LOC requires zero training and no rollout data, but relies on the WAM's latent success distribution being well-separated from failure trajectories at inference; Value MLP requires failure demonstration collection but directly learns the task-specific quality function. Their empirical comparison characterizes when WAM latent OOD scoring is sufficient versus when labeled training adds necessary discriminative power — and whether this latent-space OOD approach outperforms action-space distributional uncertainty (MG-Select-style KL).

**Mandatory RoboCasa baseline validation before committing to targets**: World2Act (arXiv 2603.10422, March 2026) reports UWM achieving 60.8% on RoboCasa using 1,000 real demonstration fine-tuning. Since UWM was trained only on DROID data and has not been fine-tuned on RoboCasa tasks, the frozen UWM baseline (no RoboCasa demos) is expected to be substantially lower — likely 10–25%. Primary performance target: ≥10pp absolute improvement over the measured frozen baseline. The 'approaching Cosmos Policy 67.1%' framing is deprioritized; the more defensible framing is 'demonstrating that WAM-specific latent OOD selection enables meaningful gains without any fine-tuning, at ≤40 H100-hours cost.'",
  "landscape": "Cosmos Policy (arXiv 2601.16163, ICLR 2026) is the primary comparison point for absolute performance. Fully fine-tunes Cosmos-Predict2-2B on robot demos (384 H100-hours ALOHA, 1,536 RoboCasa, 3,072 LIBERO). Achieves 98.5% LIBERO and 67.1% RoboCasa. Its planning mode implements Best-of-N candidate selection: generates B candidate actions, predicts future states (3 queries to world model) and values (5 queries to value function per future state, 15 total predictions per action), and executes via majority-mean aggregation. Key distinction: Cosmos Policy's authors explicitly state that demo-only training 'cannot correctly predict failure states' — rollout fine-tuning is required for the planning value function. LOC requires zero rollout data and zero weight updates; Value MLP requires ≤40 H100-hours vs. 1,536 H100-hours.

World2Act (arXiv 2603.10422, March 2026) — NEWLY ADDED. Achieves ~66% on RoboCasa (Cosmos Policy + World2Act) using only 50 real + 50 imagined demos, surpassing baseline Cosmos Policy. Method: aligns VLA action latents with world model video dynamics via a contrastive matching objective, reducing pixel-space dependence. Uses LLM-based skill decomposition to create RoboCasa-Skill and LIBERO-Skill datasets. Differentiation: World2Act requires contrastive post-training to align VLA action latents with video dynamics (modifies weights); our LOC method requires zero post-training and no weight updates — the alignment between action latents and video physics is inherited from UWM's joint pretraining. World2Act applies to VLAs requiring explicit alignment; our method exploits alignment that WAMs provide by construction.

Fast-WAM (arXiv 2603.16666, May 2026) is the critical framing reference. Test-time video generation adds only 0.5–1.9 percentage points: 97.6% LIBERO-avg and 91.8% RoboTwin without video at inference, at 190ms latency. Generates a single action trajectory with no candidate comparison. Complementary framing: Fast-WAM targets latency-critical deployment (single trajectory, fastest); our method targets success-critical tasks (B trajectories, select best via latent scoring at B × 5ms overhead).

RoVer (arXiv 2510.10975, ICLR 2026) — Generates B candidate actions from frozen VLAs, trains a 0.2B Process Reward Model that scores candidates AND predicts refinement directions. Differentiation: (1) RoVer requires training a 0.2B PRM on process labels; LOC requires zero training and Value MLP requires only a 3-layer MLP; (2) RoVer applies to VLA action tokens lacking video-physics regularization; our methods target WAM action latents z_a jointly trained with video.

Verifier-free / MG-Select (arXiv 2510.05681, ICLR 2026) — Training-free Best-of-N using KL-divergence from masked unconditional VLA distribution. 168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place. Differentiation: MG-Select measures distributional uncertainty (how much task conditioning shifts the distribution from its unconditional prior) — an action-space confidence signal. LOC measures latent OOD membership (whether z_{a,i} is in-distribution relative to success demonstrations) — a latent-space quality signal. These are mechanistically different and testable: we include MG-Select-style KL applied to WAM as an explicit baseline in the ablation grid.

FAIL-Detect (arXiv 2503.08558, RSS 2025) — NEWLY ADDED AS SUPPORTING WORK. Frames failure detection as sequential OOD detection using conformal prediction on success-only demonstration data. Uses flow-based density estimation on distilled policy input/output signals. Demonstrates that OOD detection trained only on successes reliably detects failures at execution time. Relationship to LOC: LOC applies the same OOD detection principle to WAM action latents z_a for pre-execution candidate selection (ranking among B candidates before execution rather than monitoring execution). LOC differs in: (1) direct density estimation in action latent space vs. distilled scalar signal; (2) pre-execution selection vs. execution monitoring; (3) WAM-specific latent structure from joint video-action pretraining.

EVA (arXiv 2603.17808, 2026) — NEWLY ADDED. Identifies 'executability gap' in video world models: visually coherent rollouts can violate kinematic constraints. Uses inverse dynamics model as training-time reward signal. Relevance: EVA's finding supports our decision to use action latent OOD scoring (LOC) rather than video denoising error (PCS) as the zero-training quality signal — visual coherence measured by denoising error does not imply executable actions. EVA's executability gap is complementary evidence that the latent action space (z_a) is a more direct quality substrate than the video prediction error.

WAV: World-Value-Action Model (arXiv 2604.14732, April 2026) — Integrates a trajectory value module as a new architectural component trained from scratch; iterative latent-space inference concentrating probability mass on high-value trajectories. 99.6% LIBERO, 75.6% real-world dual-arm. Differentiation: WAV modifies the architecture and trains from scratch; our method leaves all WAM weights completely frozen and adds only a lightweight scoring module (LOC: no parameters; Value MLP: ~5M parameters). WAV is plug-in-incompatible with pretrained WAMs; our method is plug-in-compatible.

Compose Your Policies! / GPC (arXiv 2510.01068) — Training-free convex composition of multiple frozen policy distributions. Different: operates at distribution level (combining score functions of multiple policies), not discrete candidate selection from a single frozen WAM; requires multiple compatible policies.

GPC-RANK (arXiv 2502.00622, IEEE RAL 2025): frozen policy + separately trained action-conditioned world model + hard argmax. Our method uses the WAM's own action latent space as the evaluation substrate — no separate world model.

When to Trust Imagination (arXiv 2605.06222, May 2026): FFDC adaptively decides action chunk sizes during single-trajectory execution. Orthogonal and combinable with our pre-execution selection.",
  "approach": "Primary backbone: UWM (github.com/WEIRDLabUW/unified-world-model, RSS 2025), whose independent per-modality diffusion timestep architecture supports action-only inference (policy mode: video timestep = T, action timestep = 0). All WAM weights frozen throughout.

**Step 0a — Frozen UWM Baseline Validation on RoboCasa (MANDATORY FIRST STEP)**: Run B=1 frozen UWM action-only inference on 50 episodes of representative RoboCasa tasks (kitchen manipulation subset). Expected baseline: 10–25% (UWM trained on DROID data only; World2Act reports 60.8% with 1,000-demo fine-tuning, confirming frozen baseline is substantially lower). Decision tree: if baseline ≥ 30%, proceed with current framing; if baseline 10–25%, confirm ≥10pp absolute improvement framing and drop all 'approaching Cosmos Policy 67.1%' language. Cost: ~2–3 H100-hours.

**Step 0b — Reference Distribution Encoding for LOC**: Encode LIBERO-90 success demos through frozen UWM in action-only mode to obtain {z_a^success}. Fit density estimators: (a) KNN nonconformity model (k=10, Euclidean distance); (b) GMM (k=3,5 components, full covariance). Split latents 80/20 train/hold-out for AUC evaluation in Step 1. Cost: ~10–15 H100-hours encoding; ~30 minutes fitting density estimator.

**Step 0c — Failure Demonstration Collection (required for Value MLP)**: (a) Primary negatives: run frozen UWM (B=1) on LIBERO-Long and validated RoboCasa tasks; expected failure rate 30–50% on RoboCasa tasks, 5–15% on LIBERO-Long, yielding 500–2,000 failure trajectories. Cost: 15–20 H100-hours. (b) Synthetic supplement: Gaussian action perturbation (σ ∈ {0.05, 0.1}) on 20% of LIBERO-90 success demos, simulate in MuJoCo, flag truncated episodes as failures. Cost: <1 H100-hour. Combined: balanced 2,000–4,000 positive / 2,000–4,000 negative training set.

**Step 1 — LOC Diagnostic (MANDATORY before main ablation)**: Validate whether WAM action latent OOD scoring correlates with ground-truth task success, and compare against video denoising error (PCS) as a secondary signal.

Protocol: Sample B=16 action-only candidates from frozen UWM on 3 RoboCasa tasks, execute each in simulation (ground-truth success/failure), compute LOC and PCS scores.

LOC metrics: (1) AUC of S_LOC as binary success predictor on held-out demos (target AUC > 0.60); (2) Spearman ρ of S_LOC with success labels (target ρ > 0.3); (3) compare KNN vs. GMM density estimators. Also compute S_PCS = ||ε − ε_θ(x_{t*}, z_{a,i}, t*)||² for the same candidates, varying t* ∈ {T/4, T/2, 3T/4} — expected to show lower AUC and ρ than LOC based on Cosmos Policy finding and EVA's executability gap evidence. Also compute MG-Select-style KL score as third comparison signal.

Expected result: LOC AUC > PCS AUC ≈ MG-Select AUC, confirming latent OOD density is more informative than video denoising error or action-space distributional uncertainty. If LOC AUC < 0.55 at all density estimator configurations, report as negative result; Value MLP becomes sole primary contribution. Decision: if LOC AUC ≥ 0.60, LOC is reported as primary zero-training method; if LOC 0.55–0.60, both methods reported with LOC as secondary; if LOC < 0.55, LOC reported as negative result with informative comparison to PCS.

This diagnostic is a key scientific contribution: it empirically tests whether WAM joint pretraining creates a success latent distribution that is more quality-discriminative than video denoising error or distributional uncertainty, directly addressing open questions about WAM latent structure.

**Step 2 — Diversity Pilot (combined with LOC diagnostic)**: Same B=16 rollouts measure: pairwise cosine distance of action latents {z_{a,i}} (target mean > 0.05; if lower, increase noise temperature T_noise ∈ {1.5, 2.0}); LOC AUC conditional on latent diversity. Binary classification accuracy on held-out demo set as latent separability sanity check.

**Step 3 — Value MLP Training**: 3-layer MLP (input: flattened z_a; output: scalar V ∈ [0,1]) trained via binary cross-entropy on balanced success/failure latents from Steps 0b and 0c. Report binary classification accuracy on held-out split (target > 75%). Cost: ~3–5 H100-hours.

**Step 4 — Inference-Time Best-of-N Planning**: At each planning step, sample B=4–8 action-only trajectories from frozen UWM.

Primary results (two methods):
- LOC selection: a_{i*} = argmin_i S_LOC(z_{a,i}) at best density estimator from diagnostic [zero weight updates, WAM-specific]
- Value MLP selection: a_{i*} = argmax_i V(z_{a,i}) [lightweight training, WAM-specific]

Comparisons (required): MG-Select-style KL scoring applied to WAM action-only inference (VLA method applied to WAM backbone, directly comparable to LOC on same benchmark); random selection (B=4–8, sanity check); single-trajectory WAM B=1 (frozen baseline).

Ablation (secondary): (a) PCS denoising error selection at best t* from diagnostic (expected to underperform LOC, confirming negative result); (b) soft MPPI w_i ∝ exp(β·V(z_{a,i})) to document action-averaging artifact; (c) action-only z_a vs. full video+action latent for LOC and Value MLP scoring.

**Ablation Grid**: B ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} (B=1 is frozen WAM single-trajectory baseline); selection method: LOC KNN vs. LOC GMM (primary zero-training) vs. Value MLP hard argmax (primary trained) vs. MG-Select-style KL (VLA method applied to WAM, key comparison) vs. PCS denoising error (expected negative result) vs. random selection (sanity check); noise temperature T_noise ∈ {1.0, 1.5, 2.0} (informed by diversity pilot); execution regime: (a) open-loop (B trajectories at episode start, execute selected) vs. (b) periodic replanning every K=5 action chunks.

**Primary hypotheses**: (H1) LOC achieves Spearman ρ > 0.3 and AUC > 0.6 in the diagnostic, confirming WAM success latents form an OOD-detectable distribution; (H2) LOC outperforms PCS and MG-Select-style KL in the diagnostic (latent OOD density > video denoising error ≈ action-space KL), with PCS showing AUC near 0.5 consistent with Cosmos Policy's finding; (H3) Value MLP achieves ≥10pp improvement over B=1 baseline on RoboCasa; (H4) LOC achieves ≥5pp improvement over B=1 with zero weight updates; (H5) Both methods outperform MG-Select-style KL applied to WAM, confirming latent quality-discrimination advantages of WAM joint pretraining over distributional uncertainty.

**Evaluation Benchmarks**: (a) Primary — RoboCasa: Cosmos Policy fine-tuned 67.1%; World2Act (Cosmos+World2Act) ~66%; frozen UWM expected 10–25% (validated in Step 0a); absolute target ≥10pp over frozen baseline. (b) Secondary — LIBERO-Long: near saturation for strong frozen WAMs (Fast-WAM 95.2%); included to characterize gain profile vs. task difficulty. (c) Baselines: B=1 frozen WAM, random selection, MG-Select-style KL applied to WAM.

DreamZero cross-WAM validation deferred to camera-ready. CoRL submission rests on UWM alone.",

# KDPE: Key Technical Details

## (1) Training Data Composition
The paper does not explicitly state whether all demonstrations or only successes are used. It references RoboMimic and MimicGen datasets but provides no filtering details about success-only selection during training.

## (2) Action Representation
KDPE uses **Cartesian space**, not latent: "actions composed of end-effector Cartesian position, orientation, and gripper state." The representation includes position (3D), rotation matrix in SO(3), and gripper aperture (1D).

## (3) Manifold Type for Kernel
The kernel handles mixed manifolds: "Euclidean differences suffice" for position and gripper, while rotations use the Lie group logarithm map with "log:SO(3)→𝔰𝔬(3)" followed by the vee operator to obtain "a representation in the tangent space."

## (4) Candidate Generation
KDPE generates N=100 trajectories: "we sample NN independent and identically distributed action trajectories" through parallel diffusion denoising processes from different noise samples conditioned on the same observation.

## (5) Benchmark Results (RoboMimic/MimicGen)
| Task | DP-C | KDPE-C |
|------|------|--------|
| Lift (ph) | 100% | 100% |
| ToolHang (ph) | 62% | **76%** |
| Assembly | 54.3% | **61%** |
| Average | 85% | **88.2%** |

KDPE-C achieved 88.2% average success rate versus DP's 85%.

## (6) Comparison to Other Selection Methods
KDPE-OOD (selecting lowest density) performed worse than KDPE, supporting outlier rejection. Tr-KDPE (trajectory-based KDE) showed "similar performance to DP, resulting in no relevant improvement." No comparisons to alternative candidate selection methods appear in the paper.

## KDPE: Kernel Density Estimation Strategy for Diffusion Policy Trajectory Selection

KDPE is a Kernel Density Estimation-based strategy that filters out potentially harmful trajectories output of Diffusion Policy while keeping a low test-time computational overhead. This work directly addresses your search query combining density estimation, action trajectory selection, and robot policy test-time performance.

### Technical Approach

The method proposes a manifold-aware kernel to model a probability density function for actions composed of end-effector Cartesian position, orientation, and gripper state.

### Performance Results

KDPE achieves better performance than Diffusion Policy on simulated single-arm RoboMimic and MimicGen tasks, and on three real robot experiments: PickPlush (a tabletop grasping task), CubeSort (a multimodal pick and place task), and CoffeeMaking (a task that requires long-horizon capabilities and precise execution).

### Publication Details

The work was published in the Proceedings of The 9th Conference on Robot Learning in 2025.

This research represents a significant recent advancement in improving robot policy execution through kernel density estimation-based trajectory filtering at test time.

{
  "title": "Latent-Distribution Candidate Selection for Frozen World Action Models: OOD Consistency Scoring and Action-Latent Value Learning",
  "change_type": "minor",
  "core_problem": "Pretrained WAMs generate a single action trajectory at inference and provide no mechanism to compare candidate futures. Adding planning capability currently requires one of three costly interventions: (1) full fine-tuning of the video model on robot demos (Cosmos Policy, ICLR 2026: 384–3,072 H100-hours); (2) training a separate action-conditioned world model alongside the frozen policy (GPC, RAL 2025); or (3) architectural co-design or RL loops (H-WM, GigaBrain RAMP, WAV). Fast-WAM (arXiv 2603.16666) demonstrates that action-only inference achieves 97.6% on LIBERO (Table 2) and 91.8% on RoboTwin (Table 1) at 190ms, motivating candidate generation from frozen WAM action-only inference rather than expensive video rollouts.

The VLA test-time compute literature (2025–2026) has addressed candidate selection for VLA architectures: RoVer (arXiv 2510.10975, ICLR 2026) trains a 0.2B Process Reward Model; MG-Select (arXiv 2510.05681, ICLR 2026) uses KL-divergence from a masked unconditional VLA distribution as a training-free confidence signal, achieving 168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place; Cosmos Policy (ICLR 2026) implements Best-of-N in its planning mode by generating B candidates and scoring each via a fine-tuned value function — but crucially, Cosmos Policy's authors report that a model trained only on demonstrations 'cannot correctly predict failure states' and that rollout fine-tuning is required to enable effective planning. KDPE (arXiv 2508.10511, CoRL 2025) applies kernel density estimation in Cartesian action space (end-effector position, orientation, gripper state) to filter Diffusion Policy trajectory outputs, achieving 88.2% vs. 85% average on RoboMimic/MimicGen — but critically, KDPE-OOD (selecting the most out-of-distribution trajectory) performed *worse* than KDPE (selecting the most typical), and KDPE uses all training demonstrations rather than a success-specific reference distribution. None of these approaches exploit WAMs' unique property: joint video-action pretraining that regularizes action latents z_a to be consistent with physically plausible visual futures, forming a success-biased latent distribution.

The central unanswered question — which VLA and Cartesian-space approaches cannot answer — is: (1) Do WAM action latents z_a, regularized by joint video-action pretraining, form a latent success distribution that is more structured and separable from failure regimes than VLA action tokens or Cartesian action representations, enabling lightweight OOD-based candidate scoring without any rollout data? (2) Is this latent OOD signal more informative than action-space distributional uncertainty (MG-Select's KL signal) or Cartesian-space density (KDPE) for candidate selection? These questions are grounded in the FAIL-Detect (arXiv 2503.08558, RSS 2025) finding that OOD detection on success-only demonstrations reliably identifies failures — but have not been applied to WAM action latents or to pre-execution candidate selection. The companion question of whether video denoising error (as opposed to latent OOD scoring) is a reliable zero-training signal is answered negatively by Cosmos Policy's own finding and by EVA (arXiv 2603.17808), which demonstrates an 'executability gap' showing that visual coherence does not predict task success.

No existing work demonstrates Best-of-N candidate selection using WAM action latents' distributional structure — either zero-training (OOD scoring) or lightweight-trained (value MLP) — without modifying any WAM weights or requiring rollout data for the zero-training path.",
  "opportunity": "UWM's independent per-modality diffusion timestep architecture (RSS 2025) natively supports action-only inference (video timestep = T, action timestep = 0), producing action latents z_a jointly pretrained with video. This creates two complementary WAM-specific approaches to candidate selection, exploiting the distributional structure of the WAM's joint video-action pretraining:

**Method 1 — Latent OOD Consistency Scoring (LOC, zero weight updates)**: Encode LIBERO-90 success demonstrations through frozen UWM in action-only mode to obtain a reference distribution {z_a^success}. Fit a lightweight density estimator — KNN-based nonconformity score (k=10) or Gaussian Mixture Model (k≤5 components) — on {z_a^success}. At inference, sample B=4–8 action-only candidates from frozen UWM, obtain latents {z_{a,1}, ..., z_{a,B}}, and score each: S_LOC(z_{a,i}) = −log p̂(z_{a,i}) (nonconformity score). Select a_{i*} = argmin_i S_LOC(z_{a,i}) (most in-distribution candidate). Total inference overhead: B × ~5ms = 20–40ms for B=4–8. Cost: ~30–60 minutes to fit density estimator on encoded latents; no WAM weight updates.

Theoretical basis: (1) FAIL-Detect (RSS 2025) proves that OOD detection on success-only demonstration data reliably detects policy failures — the success-demo distribution implicitly excludes failure modes; (2) KDPE (CoRL 2025) demonstrates in Cartesian action space that selecting the most IN-distribution trajectory improves performance, while KDPE-OOD (selecting the most out-of-distribution trajectory) performs *worse* — validating the in-distribution selection direction for LOC; (3) z_a regularized by joint video-action pretraining encodes physical plausibility co-varying with video futures, creating a success-specific latent distribution with tighter quality-discriminative geometry than both Cartesian action space (KDPE) and VLA action tokens. LOC is WAM-specific in that this geometry is a direct consequence of joint video-action pretraining absent in VLAs and not present in action-space methods.

Key differentiation from KDPE: (a) density estimation in WAM action latent space z_a, not Cartesian action space (position/orientation/gripper); (b) success-demonstrations-only reference distribution establishing a quality anchor, not all training data; (c) exploitation of WAM-specific joint pretraining regularization that aligns z_a with physical plausibility, unavailable in action-space methods; (d) B=4–8 candidates vs. KDPE's N=100, significantly cheaper inference. LOC implements success-mode selection; KDPE implements all-data-mode selection — these are mechanistically distinct quality signals.

Differentiation from MG-Select: LOC scores membership in the success demonstration distribution (latent OOD density); MG-Select measures KL divergence of task-conditioned output from masked unconditional distribution (action-space distributional uncertainty). One measures distributional membership relative to labeled success data, the other measures task-conditioning confidence.

Note on Cosmos Policy planning mode: Cosmos Policy also implements Best-of-N — generates B actions, predicts future states and values, executes the highest-value action. However, (a) requires fine-tuning a value function on rollout data (1,536 H100-hours for RoboCasa) because demonstration-only training 'cannot correctly predict failure states'; (b) 15 total forward passes per candidate. LOC requires zero rollout data, zero weight updates, and ~5ms per candidate.

Note on PCS: Video denoising error S_PCS = ||ε − ε_θ(x_{t*}, z_{a,i}, t*)||² is retained as a diagnostic comparison in Step 1, not as a primary method. Cosmos Policy's explicit finding and EVA's 'executability gap' provide strong prior evidence that denoising error is a weak candidate selection signal.

**Method 2 — Action-Latent Value MLP (≤40 H100-hours training)**: A 3-layer MLP trained on WAM action latents z_a from LIBERO-90 success demonstrations AND explicitly collected failure trajectories scores each candidate via V(z_{a,i}) ∈ [0,1]. Hard argmax Best-of-N is the primary result. Key hypothesis: z_a regularized by joint video-action pretraining is more linearly separable between success and failure regimes than raw action outputs or VLA action tokens (the latent geometry argument). Failure demonstrations collected via frozen UWM rollouts in simulation (~15–20 H100-hours) plus Gaussian-perturbed synthetic failures (<1 H100-hour).

Their empirical comparison characterizes when WAM latent OOD scoring is sufficient versus when labeled training adds necessary discriminative power — and whether this latent-space OOD approach outperforms action-space density estimation (KDPE-style) and distributional uncertainty (MG-Select-style KL).

**Mandatory RoboCasa baseline validation before committing to targets**: World2Act (arXiv 2603.10422, March 2026) reports UWM achieving 60.8% on RoboCasa using 1,000 real demonstration fine-tuning. Since UWM was trained only on DROID data and has not been fine-tuned on RoboCasa tasks, the frozen UWM baseline (no RoboCasa demos) is expected to be substantially lower — likely 10–25%. Primary performance target: ≥10pp absolute improvement over the measured frozen baseline.",
  "landscape": "Cosmos Policy (arXiv 2601.16163, ICLR 2026) is the primary comparison point for absolute performance. Fully fine-tunes Cosmos-Predict2-2B on robot demos (384 H100-hours ALOHA, 1,536 RoboCasa, 3,072 LIBERO). Achieves 98.5% LIBERO and 67.1% RoboCasa. Its planning mode implements Best-of-N candidate selection: generates B candidate actions, predicts future states (3 queries to world model) and values (5 queries to value function per future state, 15 total predictions per action), and executes via majority-mean aggregation. Key distinction: Cosmos Policy's authors explicitly state that demo-only training 'cannot correctly predict failure states' — rollout fine-tuning is required for the planning value function. LOC requires zero rollout data and zero weight updates; Value MLP requires ≤40 H100-hours vs. 1,536 H100-hours.

KDPE (arXiv 2508.10511, CoRL 2025) — NEWLY ADDED. Applies kernel density estimation to Cartesian action trajectories (end-effector position, orientation via SO(3) Lie group logarithm map, gripper state) generated by Diffusion Policy to filter multimodal outputs. Generates N=100 candidates and selects the trajectory with highest density (most typical). Achieves 88.2% vs. 85% average on RoboMimic/MimicGen tasks; real-robot evaluation on PickPlush, CubeSort, CoffeeMaking. Critical finding: KDPE-OOD (selecting the *most out-of-distribution* trajectory) performed *worse* than standard KDPE (selecting most typical) — confirming that in-distribution selection direction is correct and that the quality of the reference distribution matters. LOC differs from KDPE in three fundamental ways: (a) density estimation in the WAM's action latent space z_a rather than Cartesian action space — the latent space is regularized by joint video-action pretraining to encode physical plausibility, a quality signal absent from Cartesian position/orientation; (b) success-demonstrations-only reference distribution rather than all training data — LOC anchors the reference to task success, not behavioral frequency; (c) exploitation of WAM-specific joint pretraining that structures z_a along physical plausibility dimensions unavailable in action-space-only density methods. Additionally, LOC uses B=4–8 candidates vs. KDPE's N=100, providing a practical inference-cost advantage.

World2Act (arXiv 2603.10422, March 2026) — Achieves ~66% on RoboCasa (Cosmos Policy + World2Act) using only 50 real + 50 imagined demos. Method: aligns VLA action latents with world model video dynamics via a contrastive matching objective. Reports UWM achieves 60.8% on RoboCasa with 1,000-demo fine-tuning (confirming frozen UWM baseline is substantially lower). Differentiation: World2Act requires contrastive post-training to align VLA action latents with video dynamics (modifies weights); our LOC method requires zero post-training — the alignment is inherited from UWM's joint pretraining.

Generates a single action trajectory with no candidate comparison. Complementary framing: Fast-WAM targets latency-critical deployment (single trajectory, fastest); our method targets success-critical tasks (B trajectories, select best via latent scoring at B × 5ms overhead).

RoVer (arXiv 2510.10975, ICLR 2026) — Generates B candidate actions from frozen VLAs, trains a 0.2B Process Reward Model that scores candidates AND predicts refinement directions. Differentiation: (1) RoVer requires training a 0.2B PRM on process labels; LOC requires zero training and Value MLP requires only a 3-layer MLP; (2) RoVer applies to VLA action tokens lacking video-physics regularization; our methods target WAM action latents z_a jointly trained with video.

Verifier-free / MG-Select (arXiv 2510.05681, ICLR 2026) — Training-free Best-of-N using KL-divergence from masked unconditional VLA distribution. 168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place. Differentiation: MG-Select measures distributional uncertainty (how much task conditioning shifts the distribution from its unconditional prior) — an action-space confidence signal. LOC measures latent OOD membership (whether z_{a,i} is in-distribution relative to success demonstrations) — a latent-space quality signal. Mechanistically distinct and directly compared in ablation grid.

FAIL-Detect (arXiv 2503.08558, RSS 2025) — Frames failure detection as sequential OOD detection using conformal prediction on success-only demonstration data. Demonstrates that OOD detection trained only on successes reliably detects failures at execution time. LOC applies the same OOD detection principle to WAM action latents z_a for pre-execution candidate selection. LOC differs: (1) pre-execution selection vs. execution monitoring; (2) WAM-specific latent structure from joint video-action pretraining; (3) direct density estimation in action latent space vs. distilled scalar signal. FAIL-Detect is cited as motivating the principle; Step 1 LOC diagnostic is the first empirical test of whether this principle transfers to pre-execution WAM z_a scoring.

EVA (arXiv 2603.17808, 2026) — Identifies 'executability gap': visually coherent rollouts can violate kinematic constraints. Supports LOC over PCS: visual denoising error does not imply executable actions, while action latent OOD is more directly quality-relevant.

WAV: World-Value-Action Model (arXiv 2604.14732, April 2026) — Integrates a trajectory value module as a new architectural component trained from scratch; iterative latent-space inference concentrating probability mass on high-value trajectories. 99.6% LIBERO, 75.6% real-world dual-arm. Differentiation: WAV modifies the architecture and trains from scratch; our method leaves all WAM weights frozen. WAV is plug-in-incompatible with pretrained WAMs; our method is plug-in-compatible with any pretrained WAM.

Compose Your Policies! / GPC (arXiv 2510.01068) — Training-free convex composition of multiple frozen policy distributions. Different: operates at distribution level (combining score functions of multiple policies), not discrete candidate selection from a single frozen WAM.

GPC-RANK (arXiv 2502.00622, IEEE RAL 2025): frozen policy + separately trained action-conditioned world model + hard argmax. Our method uses the WAM's own action latent space as the evaluation substrate — no separate world model.

When to Trust Imagination (arXiv 2605.06222, May 2026): FFDC adaptively decides action chunk sizes during single-trajectory execution. Orthogonal and combinable with our pre-execution selection.",

Cost: <1 H100-hour. Combined: balanced 2,000–4,000 positive / 2,000–4,000 negative training set.

**Step 1 — LOC Diagnostic (MANDATORY before main ablation)**: Empirically tests Hypothesis H1: 'WAM joint pretraining creates a latent success distribution where S_LOC(z_a) achieves AUC > 0.60 as a binary success predictor.' This hypothesis is motivated by FAIL-Detect's principle and KDPE's finding that in-distribution selection outperforms out-of-distribution selection in action space — but Step 1 is the first empirical test of whether WAM z_a, generated via action-only inference (not execution-time monitoring as in FAIL-Detect), shows the same property in the action latent space.

Protocol: Sample B=16 action-only candidates from frozen UWM on 3 RoboCasa tasks, execute each in simulation (ground-truth success/failure), compute LOC and PCS scores.

LOC metrics: (1) AUC of S_LOC as binary success predictor on held-out demos (target AUC > 0.60); (2) Spearman ρ of S_LOC with success labels (target ρ > 0.3); (3) compare KNN vs. GMM density estimators. **Step 3 — Value MLP Training**: 3-layer MLP (input: flattened z_a; output: scalar V ∈ [0,1]) trained via binary cross-entropy on balanced success/failure latents from Steps 0b and 0c. Report binary classification accuracy on held-out split (target > 75%). Cost: ~3–5 H100-hours.
